summary: Specifies a procedure that uses several Path Computation Elements to compute shortest constrained traffic engineering paths across multiple domains. Computation proceeds backward from the destination domain toward the source. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Finding a suitable path across several network domains is difficult when each domain keeps its internal topology private. This RFC defines a backward-recursive process in which path-computation servers share boundary-to-destination options instead of full topology maps.

subtitle: How cooperating PCEs compute constrained traffic-engineering paths across several domains.

tldr.problem: A path across several IGP areas or autonomous systems may need to be optimal even though each domain keeps its topology and resource information private.
tldr.mechanism: The request travels through Path Computation Elements to the destination domain. Those PCEs build virtual shortest-path trees and pass them backward toward the source domain, where the end-to-end path is selected.
tldr.outcome: For a predetermined sequence of domains, BRPC computes the shortest constrained path while preserving topology confidentiality. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 5441 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the PCEP protocol described in RFC 5440.

sections.title: Why Per-Domain Path Computation Is Limited
sections.content:
A traffic-engineering path may cross several domains, such as IGP areas or autonomous systems. The per-domain method in RFC 5152 computes each section during signaling, but it cannot guarantee the shortest constrained end-to-end path or efficiently compute a set of diverse paths.

RFC 5441 uses the Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture. In this RFC, an optimal path means the shortest path that satisfies the constraints and would be found if the network were one flat IGP network. This requires consistent metrics across domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Computing each domain's path separately does not always produce the shortest full path. BRPC lets several path-computation servers cooperate while each domain keeps its internal network information private.

sections.title: Assumptions and Domain Boundaries
sections.content:
Each domain is assumed to support traffic engineering, and no topology or resource information is distributed between domains. The path through the domains is chosen administratively or discovered by a mechanism outside this RFC.

Some constraints can be translated at domain boundaries using local policy. A boundary node is an area border router for inter-area traffic engineering or an autonomous system border router for inter-AS traffic engineering. Each PCE serves one domain or an allowed group of consecutive domains.

The procedure guarantees an optimal path only for the specified sequence of domains. The RFC does not define how that sequence is discovered.
sections.plainLanguage: Each domain keeps its topology and resource information private. The domain sequence is known before the PCEs compute the path, and local policy may translate constraints at boundaries.

sections.title: Backward-Recursive Computation
sections.content:
The Path Computation Client (PCC) sends a PCReq to a PCE in its domain. The request moves forward through the PCE chain until it reaches the destination domain. That PCE computes a Virtual Shortest Path Tree (VSPT): shortest constrained paths from each entry boundary node to the destination.

The destination PCE returns the VSPT in a PCRep. Each preceding PCE combines the received tree with its own traffic-engineering database, computes a new tree and returns it farther backward. The source-domain PCE then selects the end-to-end path and returns it to the PCC.

A VSPT branch can be an explicit path or a loose path that identifies only the boundary node, preserving details of the domain interior. The RFC does not prescribe a specific path-computation algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The request moves from the source domain toward the destination. Each domain then adds its own path options as the response travels back to the source.

sections.title: Request Flag and Required Metric
sections.content:
BRPC adds a VSPT flag to the RP object in a PCReq. The flag is bit 25. When it is set, the PCC asks for inter-domain path computation using the BRPC procedure.

Path segments returned by downstream PCEs must include their costs. Therefore, the C flag in the PCReq's METRIC object MUST be set. Setting the RP object's O bit remains the requester's choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The request includes a flag that asks the PCE chain to use BRPC. It also requires the cost flag so the source PCE can compare path segments.

sections.title: Representing the Virtual Shortest-Path Tree
sections.content:
A VSPT is carried in a PCRep as a non-ordered list of Explicit Route Objects. Each object represents a path segment from a boundary node to the destination in the corresponding PCReq.

The RFC's example has three area border routers leading to destination D. The destination-area PCE returns one path from each border router: ABR1 through A and B to D, ABR2 directly to D, and ABR3 through C to D.
sections.plainLanguage: The VSPT is a list of path segments, one from each relevant boundary node to the destination. The list does not require a particular order.

sections.title: Diversity, Reoptimization and Metrics
sections.content:
A PCC can request diverse paths by setting the SVEC flags for link, node or shared-risk-link-group diversity. Each PCE in the chain considers that request while computing its VSPT. Computing path segments together can find diverse paths that a sequential one-path-at-a-time method may miss.

After a network change, the complete BRPC procedure must be run again to guarantee the optimal path. For reoptimization, the request can include the path already in use so PCEs avoid counting its bandwidth twice.

Inter-AS traffic engineering may require providers to normalize metrics. Combining BRPC with per-domain path computation means the end-to-end optimum is no longer guaranteed.
sections.plainLanguage: BRPC can compute diverse paths together and can be rerun after network changes. Providers may need to agree on metric values for comparisons across autonomous systems.

sections.title: Reporting an Incomplete PCE Chain
sections.content:
If a PCE does not recognize the VSPT flag, it reports an unsupported parameter using Error-Type 4 and Error-value 4. If it recognizes BRPC but does not support the procedure, it reports Error-Type 13, BRPC procedure completion failure, with Error-value 1. The PCE error is relayed to the PCC.

If a downstream PCE is unavailable, the PCE sends a negative reply with a NO-PATH object. Its NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV sets the BRPC path-computation-chain-unavailable bit.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCE reports whether it does not recognize BRPC, does not support it, or cannot reach the next PCE. This lets the requesting client know why the path computation stopped.

sections.title: Security and Topology Confidentiality
sections.content:
BRPC relies on PCEP and inherits the base protocol's risks, including spoofing, snooping, falsification and denial of service. An implementation may use policy to control which requests a PCE accepts and how many it handles.

The procedure does not increase the information exchanged between autonomous systems and preserves domain topology confidentiality. Its operation depends on cooperating PCEs exchanging path information and costs rather than complete internal topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: The PCEP security risks still apply, so PCEs may use policy to control participation. BRPC is designed to preserve each domain's topology confidentiality.
